scenes.tts: What makes the seal between cells selective, and what keeps each cell's two faces distinct? In chapter one, under gut gradients, carrier placement biased glucose toward blood. The seal decided what crossed between cells.
scenes.narration: What makes the seal between cells selective, and what keeps each cell's two faces distinct? In chapter one, under gut gradients, carrier placement biased glucose toward blood. The seal decided what crossed between cells.
scenes.caption: What makes the seal between cells selective, and what keeps each cell's two faces distinct? In chapter one, under gut gradients, carrier placement biased glucose toward blood. The seal decided what crossed between cells.
scenes.visual: Continue chapter one's 16:9 world and colour map without a reset: three pale-grey columnar gut cells fill about 65% of the frame; gut above, flowing blood below; GOLD glucose dots; BLUE sodium dots; RED sodium pumps; GREEN seals; bright WHITE apical edges; SLATE basolateral edges. A small 'schematic' label stays at bottom right throughout. On the opening question, the camera slides toward the green seal between two cells. The seal brightens, then the white apical and slate basolateral outlines glow separately. Large text appears above them: 'What makes a selective sheet?' During the link-back sentences, the camera eases back out; the white apical SGLT1 turnstiles, slate basolateral exit doors and red pumps pulse in order as gold dots move gut-to-blood, then the green seal pulses once. Ambient blood flow and drifting dots continue.

Title 'The Seal and the Sides' fades in for two seconds above the carried cell sheet. Gold and blue dots continue drifting, and the green seal shimmers gently. The question text fades out beneath the title.

scenes.tts: The seal is the tight junction, a belt where neighbouring cells meet near their apical edges. It is not solid caulk. It is a selective gate between cells.
scenes.narration: The seal is the tight junction, a belt where neighbouring cells meet near their apical edges. It is not solid caulk. It is a selective gate between cells.
scenes.caption: The seal is the tight junction, a belt where neighbouring cells meet near their apical edges. It is not solid caulk. It is a selective gate between cells.
scenes.visual: Zoom until two neighbouring cells fill the frame from apical edge to mid-height. The green contact wraps behind both cells as a continuous belt, shown by a slow three-quarter rotation of the cell pair. Label it 'tight junction'. On 'not solid caulk', a flat green plug icon appears, receives a white cross, and transforms into a green gate with several narrow openings. Small blue ions bob beside the openings; larger gold discs and a bacterium-shaped grey oval remain outside.

scenes.tts: Claudin proteins assemble into branching strands around each cell. Narrow routes through those strands can pass small ions. Meanwhile, the junction strongly restricts bacteria and larger molecules.
scenes.narration: Claudin proteins assemble into branching strands around each cell. Narrow routes through those strands can pass small ions. Meanwhile, the junction strongly restricts bacteria and larger molecules.
scenes.caption: Claudin proteins assemble into branching strands around each cell. Narrow routes through those strands can pass small ions. Meanwhile, the junction strongly restricts bacteria and larger molecules.
scenes.visual: The green belt unfolds into a large flat cartoon strip occupying most of the frame. Labelled GREEN blocks marked 'claudin' join into branching lines; this is a labelled-block cartoon, not a molecular structure. One narrow opening repeatedly admits single BLUE ion dots. A larger GOLD disc and the grey bacterium-shaped oval bump gently against the strand and drift away. Keep 'schematic' visible.

scenes.tts: The small intestine needs some sodium and water to cross between cells, so its junctions are relatively leaky. The bladder needs a tighter barrier. Different epithelia tune this gate for different jobs.
scenes.narration: The small intestine needs some sodium and water to cross between cells, so its junctions are relatively leaky. The bladder needs a tighter barrier. Different epithelia tune this gate for different jobs.
scenes.caption: The small intestine needs some sodium and water to cross between cells, so its junctions are relatively leaky. The bladder needs a tighter barrier. Different epithelia tune this gate for different jobs.
scenes.visual: Refold the cartoon strip into the same three-cell sheet. The label above the sheet reads 'small intestine'; a modest stream of BLUE sodium dots and simple CYAN water drops passes through the green gates. The label then morphs to 'bladder'; the same gate narrows and nearly all dots turn aside. A two-position slider at the top moves from 'relatively leaky' toward 'tighter'. No numerical permeability is implied; 'schematic' remains visible.

scenes.tts: How can we measure this gate? Grow cells as a sheet on a porous filter. Put one electrode above and another below, then pass current. If resistance falls, must glucose be leaking through?
scenes.narration: How can we measure this gate? Grow cells as a sheet on a porous filter. Put one electrode above and another below, then pass current. If resistance falls, must glucose be leaking through?
scenes.caption: How can we measure this gate? Grow cells as a sheet on a porous filter. Put one electrode above and another below, then pass current. If resistance falls, must glucose be leaking through?
scenes.visual: The gut and blood bands morph into upper and lower fluid chambers while the same three cells settle onto a thick porous filter. Two large electrode cartoons slide into the chambers, one above and one below. A simple meter marked 'resistance' rises at the right as tiny BLUE ion dots move in response to the current. On the final question, a GOLD glucose dot appears beside the meter with a question mark. Question text fills the top: 'Lower resistance = glucose leak?'

Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the question 'Lower resistance = glucose leak?' and the gold glucose dot. The meter needle trembles slightly, blue ions drift slowly, and the green junction shimmers. No other change occurs.

scenes.tts: No. This reading is transepithelial electrical resistance, or T E E R. It reports how easily ions cross the whole sheet. It cannot name the ion or route, or say whether larger molecules leak.
scenes.narration: No. This reading is transepithelial electrical resistance, or TEER. It reports how easily ions cross the whole sheet. It cannot name the ion or route, or say whether larger molecules leak.
scenes.caption: No. This reading is transepithelial electrical resistance, or TEER. It reports how easily ions cross the whole sheet. It cannot name the ion or route, or say whether larger molecules leak.
scenes.visual: The question mark becomes a clear 'No'. The gold glucose dot slides away from the meter. The meter label expands to 'TEER: ionic resistance'. BLUE ion dots take two animated paths: some between cells at the green junction and some through a cell. Three small question tags appear beside the paths, one at a time: 'which ion?', 'which route?', 'larger molecules?'. Each remains unanswered.

scenes.tts: Current may cross between cells or pass through them. A low reading can reflect selective ion pores, broader leaks, or breaks. Telling them apart takes other experiments, set as a design problem below.
scenes.narration: Current may cross between cells or pass through them. A low reading can reflect selective ion pores, broader leaks, or breaks. Telling them apart takes other experiments, set as a design problem below.
scenes.caption: Current may cross between cells or pass through them. A low reading can reflect selective ion pores, broader leaks, or breaks. Telling them apart takes other experiments, set as a design problem below.
scenes.visual: Keep the filter insert and meter. The meter needle sits low. At the same green junction, three large labelled possibility tokens fan out in sequence, each a transformation of the junction: 'pore' (the gate keeps its narrow openings), 'broader leak' (the openings widen) and 'break' (a gap opens between the cells). Each token carries a question mark; none is chosen. A small tag 'design problem below' appears on the last sentence. Do not show tracers or test methods. No measured curve or invented number is shown.

scenes.tts: The seal is often called a fence, said to stop membrane proteins drifting between the two faces. How well it fences is tested in the text below. Cells also mark territories with proteins, and traffic delivers cargo to each face.
scenes.narration: The seal is often called a fence, said to stop membrane proteins drifting between the two faces. How well it fences is tested in the text below. Cells also mark territories with proteins, and traffic delivers cargo to each face.
scenes.caption: The seal is often called a fence, said to stop membrane proteins drifting between the two faces. How well it fences is tested in the text below. Cells also mark territories with proteins, and traffic delivers cargo to each face.
scenes.visual: The laboratory chambers morph back into the original gut, cell and blood world. The WHITE apical and SLATE basolateral outlines return. A small fence icon sits at the green boundary; a question mark appears beside it with the words 'tested below'. The fence neither fades nor is confirmed. Inside the middle cell, coloured delivery vesicles travel on curved paths: one docks only at the white apical edge and another only at the slate basolateral edge.

scenes.tts: In the standard scheme, Crumbs marks the apical side, while Scribble marks the basolateral side. The Par complex sits near their boundary. These groups are thought to restrain one another, while polarized traffic places carriers.
scenes.narration: In the standard scheme, Crumbs marks the apical side, while Scribble marks the basolateral side. The Par complex sits near their boundary. These groups are thought to restrain one another, while polarized traffic places carriers.
scenes.caption: In the standard scheme, Crumbs marks the apical side, while Scribble marks the basolateral side. The Par complex sits near their boundary. These groups are thought to restrain one another, while polarized traffic places carriers.
scenes.visual: On the middle cell, three large labelled colour bands appear without molecular detail: a WHITE 'Crumbs' band along the apical edge, a SLATE 'Scribble' band along the basolateral edge, and a MAGENTA 'Par' bracket (not green, which is reserved for the seal) at their boundary. As each band expands slightly, the others stop at its border. Delivery vesicles continue moving; an SGLT1 turnstile settles into the white top and a RED pump settles into the slate base.

scenes.tts: Below the seal, an adherens junction couples neighbouring actin belts. Desmosomes link keratin networks against stretching. Gap junctions pass ions and small molecules between cytosols.
scenes.narration: Below the seal, an adherens junction couples neighbouring actin belts. Desmosomes link keratin networks against stretching. Gap junctions pass ions and small molecules between cytosols.
scenes.caption: Below the seal, an adherens junction couples neighbouring actin belts. Desmosomes link keratin networks against stretching. Gap junctions pass ions and small molecules between cytosols.
scenes.visual: Camera pans down the existing contact between two cells. Keep the GREEN tight junction at the top. An ORANGE adherens belt appears below it and tugs matching actin ropes in both cells. A PURPLE desmosome spot weld appears lower and catches thicker keratin cables as the cells pull apart gently. A CYAN gap-junction channel appears lower still; two tiny dots pass directly from one cytosol to the other. Labels are each two words or fewer.

scenes.tts: At the base, hemidesmosomes connect keratin to the basement membrane. Each junction has a different job. Together they let a one-cell-thick sheet stay selective, strong, connected, and anchored.
scenes.narration: At the base, hemidesmosomes connect keratin to the basement membrane. Each junction has a different job. Together they let a one-cell-thick sheet stay selective, strong, connected, and anchored.
scenes.caption: At the base, hemidesmosomes connect keratin to the basement membrane. Each junction has a different job. Together they let a one-cell-thick sheet stay selective, strong, connected, and anchored.
scenes.visual: Pan to the cell base. A RED-BROWN hemidesmosome anchor clips the keratin cables to a broad tan mat labelled 'basement membrane'. Pull back to reveal the complete junction stack as five glowing marks down the same pair of cells. They pulse one by one with short job labels: 'select', 'grip', 'resist', 'connect', 'anchor'. The sheet bends gently but stays intact.

scenes.tts: Back in the gut, S G L T one stays apical while the pump stays basolateral. The selective seal controls the path between cells, while deeper junctions keep the sheet intact.
scenes.narration: Back in the gut, SGLT1 stays apical while the pump stays basolateral. The selective seal controls the path between cells, while deeper junctions keep the sheet intact.
scenes.caption: Back in the gut, SGLT1 stays apical while the pump stays basolateral. The selective seal controls the path between cells, while deeper junctions keep the sheet intact.
scenes.visual: Return to chapter one's full three-cell view. GOLD glucose dots pass through apical SGLT1 turnstiles and leave toward blood; BLUE sodium dots are ejected by RED basolateral pumps. At the same time, a few BLUE ions cross the GREEN paracellular gate, while the orange, purple, cyan and basal anchors hold steady. A large gut-to-blood arrow grows through the middle cell without covering the junctions.

scenes.tts: That is the rule: epithelial barriers are built by division of labour. A gate, distinct faces, grips, anchors, and channels work together, but they are not interchangeable.
scenes.narration: That is the rule: epithelial barriers are built by division of labour. A gate, distinct faces, grips, anchors, and channels work together, but they are not interchangeable.
scenes.caption: That is the rule: epithelial barriers are built by division of labour. A gate, distinct faces, grips, anchors, and channels work together, but they are not interchangeable.
scenes.visual: The full sheet remains moving behind five large labelled icons arranged along one cell: 'selective gate' at the green seal, 'distinct faces' across the white and slate outlines, 'grip' at the adherens belt, 'anchor' at the base, and 'channel' at the gap junction. Each icon briefly takes its turn while the others stay in place. They then lock together around the intact sheet.

End card over the dimmed but still moving gut-sheet world. Large centred white text: 'Selective gates, distinct faces, and strong junctions divide the work.' Gold and blue dots drift slowly behind the line; the green seal and lower junctions pulse once in order.
